mainEntity.name: What if my payment is less than the monthly interest?

acceptedAnswer.text:
The calculator will warn you — the balance grows rather than shrinks, and you'll never pay
              it off. Increase your payment above the monthly interest charge.

mainEntity.name: Does this factor in new purchases on the card?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Stop using the card for new purchases if you want this payoff date to hold.

mainEntity.name: How long does paying off a $5,000 credit card at 24% APR take?

acceptedAnswer.text: At a 2 percent minimum of about 100 dollars per month, roughly 8 years and over 4,400 dollars in interest. At 200 dollars per month, about 3 years and 2,100 dollars in interest.

mainEntity.name: Is it better to pay off credit cards or save an emergency fund first?

acceptedAnswer.text: Keep about 500 to 1,000 dollars as a mini emergency fund, then attack high-APR debt, then rebuild savings. Clearing a 24 percent APR card mathematically beats earning 4-5 percent in savings.

mainEntity.name: Does making multiple small payments during the month help?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Interest is calculated on the daily balance, so two 100-dollar payments reduce the average daily balance more than one 200-dollar payment at month-end.

mainEntity.name: What is a balance transfer and should I use one?

acceptedAnswer.text: Moving your balance to a card with a 0 percent intro APR, usually 12 to 21 months with a 3-5 percent transfer fee. It saves interest if you clear the balance during the intro window.

mainEntity.name: Will making extra payments improve my credit score faster?

acceptedAnswer.text: Lower balances reduce your credit-utilization ratio, a major score factor. The effect usually shows within one to two statement cycles of the lower balance being reported.

mainEntity.name: Does this calculator work for store cards and gas cards?

acceptedAnswer.text: Any revolving line with an APR works. Some store cards use deferred-interest promotions that charge retroactive back-interest if the balance is not paid in full by the promo end date.

mainEntity.name: Are there fees the calculator ignores?

acceptedAnswer.text: Annual fees, late fees up to roughly 41 dollars, penalty APRs up to 29.99 percent, foreign transaction fees, and cash-advance fees. Any of these change the payoff plan.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I pay off my card and stop using it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Keep the card open to preserve credit age and utilization. Most issuers close accounts after 24 or more months of inactivity, so put a small recurring subscription on it and auto-pay in full.

mainEntity.name: How many business days are in a year?

acceptedAnswer.text: About 260 weekdays, minus 11 federal holidays = roughly 249 business days, though this varies with weekend placement around holidays.

mainEntity.name: What are the 11 US federal holidays?

acceptedAnswer.text: New Year's Day, MLK Day, Presidents' Day, Memorial Day, Juneteenth, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving, and Christmas.

mainEntity.name: What happens when a federal holiday falls on a weekend?

acceptedAnswer.text: Federal holidays falling on Saturday are observed the prior Friday; those on Sunday are observed Monday.

mainEntity.name: How are leap years handled?

acceptedAnswer.text: Every 4 years has 366 days, except century years not divisible by 400 (1700, 1800, 1900 were common years; 2000 was a leap year).

mainEntity.name: Are calendar days the same as business days?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — a "calendar day" includes weekends and holidays; a "business day" excludes Saturdays, Sundays, and federal holidays. Contracts must specify which.

mainEntity.name: How do I add X days to a date?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add directly to the day-of-month, with automatic month/year rollovers. This calculator handles the arithmetic and leap-day transitions.

mainEntity.name: What date-count convention does finance use?

acceptedAnswer.text: 30/360 for some bonds, Actual/Actual for US Treasuries, and Actual/365-fixed for most adjustable-rate loans — the convention names the math.

mainEntity.name: How do I count excluding the end date?

acceptedAnswer.text: Default behavior excludes the end date — result is the strict difference. Include it by adding one to the count (common for hotel-night or exam-window counting).

mainEntity.name: Does DST affect day counting?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — DST shifts hours within a day, not the day count. Only cross-timezone hour calculations need DST handling.

mainEntity.name: What is the fairest way to deliver a "30-day notice"?

acceptedAnswer.text: Specify calendar days (most common default), a specific date ("by March 15"), or business days for corporate contracts. Ambiguity triggers disputes.

mainEntity.name: What is the rectangle diagonal formula?

acceptedAnswer.text: d = √(length² + width²), the Pythagorean theorem. A 16×9 cm rectangle has a diagonal of √337 ≈ 18.36 cm.

mainEntity.name: What is a square's diagonal?

acceptedAnswer.text: d = s × √2. A 10 cm square has a diagonal of about 14.14 cm.

mainEntity.name: What is the 3-4-5 rule in carpentry?

acceptedAnswer.text: If legs are in a 3:4 ratio, the diagonal is exactly 5 units — a fast integer right-angle check used on decks, frames, and foundations.

mainEntity.name: How do I check if a room is square?

acceptedAnswer.text: Measure both diagonals corner-to-corner. If they match within 0.5 percent (about 3-4 mm per meter), the room is square.

mainEntity.name: How is TV screen size measured?

acceptedAnswer.text: As the diagonal in inches, excluding the bezel. A "55-inch" TV has a 55-inch panel diagonal — roughly 47.9 × 26.96 inches at 16:9 aspect.

mainEntity.name: What is the space diagonal of a 3D box?

acceptedAnswer.text: The inside corner-to-opposite-corner line, d = √(l² + w² + h²). Useful for shipping — the longest item to fit inside a box.

mainEntity.name: How many diagonals does a polygon have?

acceptedAnswer.text: Formula: n(n−3) ÷ 2. A pentagon has 5; a hexagon 9; a decagon 35.

mainEntity.name: Are a rhombus's diagonals perpendicular?

acceptedAnswer.text: Always — they bisect each other at right angles. Given one diagonal p and side a, the other is q = 2 × √(a² − (p/2)²).

mainEntity.name: How do I find a parallelogram diagonal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Using the law of cosines: d = √(a² + b² − 2ab·cos θ), where a and b are adjacent sides and θ the included angle.

mainEntity.name: What is the diagonal of a cube?

acceptedAnswer.text: d = s × √3 — the space-diagonal formula when all three dimensions are equal.

mainEntity.name: What exactly is FIRE?

acceptedAnswer.text: Financial Independence, Retire Early — saving aggressively (often 50 to 70 percent of income) to reach a number that allows living off investment returns indefinitely, typically 20 to 40 years earlier than traditional retirement.

mainEntity.name: What does the 4 percent rule mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: Based on the Trinity Study, withdrawing 4 percent of the initial retirement balance (inflation-adjusted thereafter) had a 95 percent historical success rate over 30-year periods in US markets 1926-1995.

mainEntity.name: Is the 4 percent rule still valid?

acceptedAnswer.text: Debated — modern forecast returns are lower, and FIRE horizons often exceed 30 years. Many practitioners now plan for 3.0 to 3.5 percent, which raises the savings target proportionally.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between Lean FIRE and Fat FIRE?

acceptedAnswer.text: Lean FIRE targets a minimalist lifestyle (typically under 45,000 dollars annual spend), Fat FIRE accommodates a higher-spending lifestyle (over 100,000 dollars). Barista FIRE uses part-time work to cover some costs.

mainEntity.name: How much do I need to save for FIRE?

acceptedAnswer.text: Annual spending × 25 at the 4 percent rule, × about 33 at a 3 percent rule. Cutting annual spending by 1,000 dollars reduces the required number by roughly 25,000 dollars.

mainEntity.name: What is the biggest obstacle for FIRE?

acceptedAnswer.text: Healthcare before Medicare — individual plans for a 45-year-old in the US can run 1,000 to 2,500 dollars per month, often the single largest budget line after housing.

mainEntity.name: Can I access 401(k) money before 59½ without penalty?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, via a Roth conversion ladder (5-year pipeline) or the Rule of 55 (separate from employer at age 55+), plus SEPP / 72(t) substantially-equal-periodic payments. All have trade-offs — plan carefully.

mainEntity.name: Does home equity count toward my FIRE number?

acceptedAnswer.text: Generally no — you cannot spend your house. Only liquid invested assets (brokerage, retirement, HSA) that produce cash flow should be counted.

mainEntity.name: How important is the savings rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dominant — the gap between savings rate and spending rate determines years to FI far more than returns. A 50 percent savings rate leads to FI in roughly 17 years; a 20 percent rate takes about 37 years.

mainEntity.name: What about inflation during a long retirement?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 4 percent withdrawal rule is inflation-adjusted by design. For longer horizons (40+ years), plan for 3 percent-plus annual spend growth or consider a flexible-spending approach (guardrails).

mainEntity.name: How many liters in a US gallon?

acceptedAnswer.text: Exactly 3.785411784 liters (1 US liquid gallon). The US and Imperial (UK) gallon differ — Imperial is 4.54609 liters.

mainEntity.name: What is a dry gallon?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rarely used US dry-goods measure equal to about 4.405 liters — between the US liquid and Imperial gallon. Mostly historical.

mainEntity.name: How many liters in a UK gallon?

acceptedAnswer.text: 4.54609 liters — about 20 percent more than the US gallon. UK "mpg" figures look 20 percent better partly for this reason.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert mpg to L/100km?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use 235.215 ÷ mpg (US gallons). A 25 mpg US car is about 9.4 L/100km. This calculator includes fuel-price conversion.

mainEntity.name: Why does the US still use gallons?

acceptedAnswer.text: US Customary System predates metric and remains legally defined alongside metric under the 1988 Omnibus Trade Act.

mainEntity.name: How many gallons in a liter?

acceptedAnswer.text: About 0.264 US gallons. Divide liters by 3.7854 to get gallons.

mainEntity.name: What is a US quart?

acceptedAnswer.text: One-fourth of a US gallon — 0.946353 liters, very close to a liter. Milk, motor oil, and paint are commonly sold in quarts.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert fuel price per gallon to per liter?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide price per gallon by 3.7854. For example, $3.50 per gallon = about $0.925 per liter.

mainEntity.name: Is a beer barrel the same as an oil barrel?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — a US beer barrel is 31 US gallons (117.3 L); an oil barrel is 42 US gallons (158.99 L). Confusing them causes ordering errors.

mainEntity.name: Why does "50 mpg UK" differ from "50 mpg US"?

acceptedAnswer.text: UK imperial gallons are 20 percent larger, so a "50 mpg" UK figure means about 42 mpg US for the same fuel economy.

mainEntity.name: What is overtime under the FLSA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Nonexempt employees receive 1.5× their regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. Some states (California) add daily overtime after 8 hours.

mainEntity.name: What is California daily overtime?

acceptedAnswer.text: Time-and-a-half after 8 hours in a workday, double-time after 12. This differs from the federal weekly-only rule.

mainEntity.name: Are lunch breaks paid?

acceptedAnswer.text: Genuine unpaid meal breaks (30+ minutes, fully relieved of duty) are not. Short rest breaks of 5 to 20 minutes must be paid under FLSA.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert decimal hours to H:MM?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply the decimal portion by 60. Example: 7.75 hours = 7 hours 45 minutes.

mainEntity.name: What is the 2026 federal minimum wage?

acceptedAnswer.text: 7.25 dollars per hour federally (unchanged since 2009), though many states and cities set higher minimums — Washington state and DC lead around 16-17 dollars.

mainEntity.name: How does the tipped-employee minimum work?

acceptedAnswer.text: Employers may pay tipped employees as little as 2.13 dollars per hour federally, if tips bring them to at least the federal minimum; otherwise the employer tops up.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate hourly rate from annual salary?

acceptedAnswer.text: Annual salary ÷ 2,080 (40 hours × 52 weeks). An 85,000 dollar salary is about 40.87 dollars per hour.

mainEntity.name: Are paid holidays counted toward overtime?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not federally — overtime counts worked hours only. Some union contracts count holiday pay toward the weekly 40-hour threshold.

mainEntity.name: How is unpaid break time handled?

acceptedAnswer.text: Subtracted from total shift time before hours are counted. Verify break deductions are accurate — this is a common payroll error.

mainEntity.name: What happens with an overnight shift?

acceptedAnswer.text: Clock-in at 10 PM and clock-out at 6 AM spans midnight — the calculator treats this as 8 hours, not a negative number.

mainEntity.name: What is Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA)?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dollar-Cost Averaging is investing a fixed dollar amount at regular intervals (e.g., monthly) regardless of share price. It reduces the impact of short-term volatility and removes the need to time the market.

mainEntity.name: What is the historical average return of the S&P 500?

acceptedAnswer.text: Over the past 50+ years the S&P 500 has returned roughly 10% annualized before inflation, or about 7% real after inflation. Individual decades can differ dramatically from that average.

mainEntity.name: How much will $1,000 a month grow in 25 years?

acceptedAnswer.text: At a 10% nominal annual return, $1,000 a month for 25 years grows to roughly $1.27M, comprising about $309,000 in contributions and the rest in compounded growth. Actual results depend on real market returns.

mainEntity.name: What is a wealth multiplier?

acceptedAnswer.text: The wealth multiplier is the ending portfolio value divided by total contributions. A multiplier of 4.1x means every deposited dollar became $4.10 thanks to compounding.

mainEntity.name: Should I invest a lump sum or monthly?

acceptedAnswer.text: Historically, investing a lump sum immediately has slightly outperformed averaging it in, because markets rise more often than they fall. Monthly investing (DCA) reduces regret risk and matches how most people receive income.

mainEntity.name: What expense ratio should I use?

acceptedAnswer.text: Enter your fund’s actual expense ratio. Broad S&P 500 index funds commonly charge 0.02%–0.16%, while some mutual funds charge 0.5%–1%. Even small fees compound into large dollar differences over decades.

mainEntity.name: Does this calculator account for inflation?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Results are in nominal dollars. To approximate real (inflation-adjusted) growth, run the projection at 7% instead of 10%, which mirrors the S&P 500’s long-run real return.

mainEntity.name: Is monthly investing better during a market crash?

acceptedAnswer.text: Crashes are when DCA buys the most shares at the lowest prices. Investors who keep contributing through downturns historically recover faster once markets rebound.

mainEntity.name: How does the annual step-up work?

acceptedAnswer.text: The step-up increases your monthly deposit by a fixed percentage each year (e.g., 5%), mirroring raises. Later, larger contributions still benefit from the remaining compounding years, raising the final value materially.

mainEntity.name: What index funds can I use for DCA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common choices include VOO, VTI, FXAIX, SWPPX, and ITOT. Choose a broad, low-cost, diversified fund and automate monthly purchases through your broker’s recurring-investment feature.

mainEntity.name: How much house can I afford?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 28/36 rule: housing costs should stay under 28 percent of gross monthly income, and total debt under 36 percent. On an 85,000 dollar salary that suggests a mortgage payment near 1,980 dollars, including taxes and insurance.

mainEntity.name: What is PMI and when can I remove it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Private Mortgage Insurance is 0.3 to 1.5 percent of the loan per year, required on conventional loans below 20 percent down. It is removable once you reach 20 percent equity through payments or an appraisal.

mainEntity.name: Should I choose a 15-year or 30-year mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 30-year has lower monthly payments but much more total interest; the 15-year usually runs 0.5 to 0.75 percentage points lower and cuts total interest by more than half. Choose 30-year if cash flow is tight, 15-year to save.

mainEntity.name: What are closing costs on a US mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Typically 2 to 5 percent of the loan amount — appraisal, title, origination, points, escrow, and recording fees. Always compare the Loan Estimates from at least three lenders.

mainEntity.name: What is the current conforming loan limit for 2025?

acceptedAnswer.text: 806,500 dollars in most US counties, higher in high-cost areas. Loans above this are "jumbo" mortgages with stricter requirements.

mainEntity.name: How does an ARM (adjustable-rate mortgage) work?

acceptedAnswer.text: The rate is fixed for an initial period (5, 7, or 10 years), then adjusts annually based on an index plus a margin. Rate caps limit yearly adjustment, but resets can still jump payments significantly.

mainEntity.name: Is it better to put 20 percent down or invest the extra cash?

acceptedAnswer.text: Twenty percent down avoids PMI, cutting monthly cost. But if the mortgage rate is 5 percent and your investment return is 7 percent, investing extra may outperform — factoring in liquidity and risk preference.

mainEntity.name: How much does property tax add to a mortgage payment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Typically 1 to 2 percent of home value per year, escrowed in monthly installments. In New Jersey the average is over 2 percent, in Hawaii under 0.4 percent.

mainEntity.name: What credit score do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Conventional loans require a minimum score of 620; FHA loans accept 580 with 3.5 percent down (500 with 10 percent). Better credit means a lower rate — a 740-versus-680 score difference is roughly 0.5 to 1 percentage point.

mainEntity.name: Can I pay off my mortgage early?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most conforming loans have no prepayment penalty (verify in your note). Extra principal payments slash total interest — an extra 100 dollars per month on a 30-year 360,000 dollar loan saves roughly 35,000 dollars.

No. Each state sets its own rate (or has none at all — TX, FL, WA, etc.). Add your state's

mainEntity.name: Are 401(k) contributions subtracted before tax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, for traditional 401(k). Roth 401(k) is post-tax and would not reduce today's taxable wage.

mainEntity.name: How accurate is this paycheck calculator?

acceptedAnswer.text: Within about 2 percent for federal tax and FICA on a simple W-4 with no extra withholding. Accuracy drops with nonstandard W-4 elections, itemized deductions, or noncash benefits.

mainEntity.name: Why is my first paycheck lower than later ones?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually proration — you worked fewer hours that period, or benefits start the following month. Health premiums are sometimes charged twice in a month with three biweekly pay periods.

mainEntity.name: What is the Social Security wage base for 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: Wages stop accruing the 6.2 percent Social Security portion above the annual wage base, but continue to accrue the 1.45 percent Medicare portion (and the 0.9 percent Additional Medicare tax above 200,000 dollars single or 250,000 dollars married).

mainEntity.name: What is the Additional Medicare Tax?

acceptedAnswer.text: 0.9 percent on employee wages above 200,000 dollars single or 250,000 dollars married filing jointly, on top of the normal 1.45 percent Medicare. Employers withhold it automatically once wages cross the threshold.

mainEntity.name: Do I get taxes back at year-end if I overpaid?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Overwithheld amounts are refunded after filing your federal return, typically within 21 days of the IRS accepting an e-filed return.

mainEntity.name: Is bonus income taxed differently?

acceptedAnswer.text: Supplemental wages can be withheld at a flat 22 percent federal rate (37 percent above 1 million dollars), but actual tax at filing is based on your bracket. Overwithheld bonus tax is refunded at filing.

mainEntity.name: Do Roth 401(k) contributions reduce my paycheck now?

acceptedAnswer.text: They reduce take-home pay more than traditional 401(k) because they are post-tax, but produce tax-free qualified withdrawals at retirement. This calculator models traditional 401(k) only.

mainEntity.name: Are FSA or HSA contributions pre-tax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Payroll-deducted FSA and HSA contributions reduce taxable wages for both FICA and federal income tax, effectively saving the 7.65 percent FICA share plus your marginal rate.

mainEntity.name: How much do I need to retire?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 25-times rule: annual spending × 25. Spending 60,000 dollars a year suggests a 1.5 million dollar nest egg, adjusted for inflation (to this year's dollars).

mainEntity.name: When should I claim Social Security?

acceptedAnswer.text: Claiming at 62 permanently reduces benefits; full retirement age is 67; delaying past 67 adds 8 percent per year up to age 70. For higher earners, delaying is often one of the best guaranteed-return deals available.

mainEntity.name: How is Social Security calculated?

acceptedAnswer.text: Based on your highest 35 years of indexed earnings. Zero-earning years count as zeros, which is why career gaps, especially early, permanently reduce the benefit.

mainEntity.name: Is Social Security taxed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Up to 85 percent of benefits can be taxable for higher-income retirees; some states also tax benefits. Plan with your after-tax benefit, not the gross number.

mainEntity.name: What should my retirement withdrawal rate be?

acceptedAnswer.text: The classic 4 percent rule; more conservative modern planning uses 3.0 to 3.5 percent, reflecting lower forecast returns and longer lifespans.

mainEntity.name: When should I start Medicare?

acceptedAnswer.text: At 65. Missing the 7-month initial enrollment window triggers permanent late penalties (Part B up to 10 percent per year missed). COBRA alone doesn't satisfy this window — enroll by 65 even if still working.

mainEntity.name: How much should healthcare before Medicare cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Retirees aged 62-64 without employer coverage can expect 800 to 2,000 dollars per month for ACA-compliant plans, varying widely by subsidy eligibility.

mainEntity.name: What is a Roth conversion ladder?

acceptedAnswer.text: Converting portions of traditional IRA/401(k) to Roth over several low-income years creates a tax-free withdrawal pipeline accessible penalty-free after 5 years — the standard bridge for early retirees.

mainEntity.name: How long does my retirement savings need to last?

acceptedAnswer.text: A healthy 65-year-old man has roughly a 50 percent chance of reaching 85; a woman about 55 percent. Plan to age 95 for a conservative margin.

mainEntity.name: What is sequence-of-returns risk?

acceptedAnswer.text: A bear market immediately before or after retirement can permanently reduce safe withdrawal capacity. Mitigation: a cash or bond reserve covering 2-3 years of spending.

mainEntity.name: What is the 2026 Roth IRA contribution limit?

acceptedAnswer.text: 7,500 dollars under age 50, 8,500 dollars at age 50 and older with the catch-up. The limit applies to combined Traditional plus Roth IRA contributions.

mainEntity.name: What is the income limit for contributing?

acceptedAnswer.text: For 2026, the single-filer MAGI phase-out begins around 153,000-168,000 dollars; for MFJ it is roughly double. Above the upper limit you cannot contribute directly — use a backdoor Roth.

mainEntity.name: What is a backdoor Roth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Contribute non-deductibly to a Traditional IRA (no income limit), then convert to Roth. Watch the pro-rata rule — if you hold pre-tax IRA money anywhere, a portion of the conversion is taxable.

mainEntity.name: When can I withdraw without penalty?

acceptedAnswer.text: Contributions can be withdrawn anytime, tax- and penalty-free. Earnings require age 59½ and an account held at least 5 years. Exceptions include first home (up to 10,000 dollars of earnings), disability, and qualified education expenses.

mainEntity.name: Are Roth IRAs subject to RMDs?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — no Required Minimum Distributions during the original owner's lifetime. This is a major estate-planning advantage over traditional IRAs and 401(k)s.

mainEntity.name: Can I convert a traditional IRA to Roth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — a Roth conversion is taxable on the pre-tax portion converted. Many do "ladder" conversions in low-income years (retirement gap years before RMD age) to permanently minimize lifetime taxes.

mainEntity.name: Tax-free growth: does that mean no tax on dividends?

acceptedAnswer.text: Correct — dividends, interest, and capital gains inside a Roth IRA are never taxed, even at withdrawal, as long as it is a qualified distribution.

mainEntity.name: What is the 5-year rule?

acceptedAnswer.text: Earnings must have been in a Roth account at least 5 tax years before a qualified (tax- and penalty-free) withdrawal of earnings at 59½. Each conversion has its own separate 5-year clock.

mainEntity.name: Roth IRA or traditional IRA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Roth when you expect to be in a higher tax bracket at retirement, traditional when lower. Most young workers are better served by Roth — locking today's low rates before tax brackets rise on large balances.

mainEntity.name: Can my spouse contribute without earned income?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — a "spousal IRA" contribution up to the annual limit based on the working spouse's earned income, filed jointly, as both partners' combined IRA contributions stay under the limit.

mainEntity.name: Which states have no sales tax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Five: Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon. Alaska allows local-option sales taxes in some boroughs.

mainEntity.name: What is the highest combined sales tax in the US?

acceptedAnswer.text: Louisiana and Tennessee top the combined state plus average local rates above 9.5 percent. Some individual jurisdictions in California and Alabama exceed 10 percent.

mainEntity.name: Do online purchases have sales tax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — after the 2018 South Dakota v. Wayfair decision, most states collect sales tax from online sellers above an economic-nexus threshold, commonly 100,000 dollars in sales or 200 transactions.

mainEntity.name: Is shipping taxable?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the state. In some states (e.g. New York), separately stated shipping is not taxable; in others (e.g. Texas) it is.

mainEntity.name: Are groceries taxed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most states exempt groceries or apply a reduced rate, but a handful (Alabama, Mississippi, South Dakota, others) apply the full sales tax to food.

mainEntity.name: What is "use tax"?

acceptedAnswer.text: The companion tax owed when you buy in a no-sales-tax state (or online without paying tax) and use the item in your home state. It is filed on your state income tax return and rarely enforced for small purchases.

mainEntity.name: How do I reverse-calculate tax from a total?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide the tax-included total by 1 plus the rate. For example, 108.25 dollars at 8.25 percent = 108.25 ÷ 1.0825 = 100 dollars pre-tax, with 8.25 dollars tax.

mainEntity.name: Are services taxed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Varies — professional services (legal, medical, accounting) are generally not taxed, but some states (New Mexico, Hawaii, South Dakota) tax most services. Repair services are taxed in several states.

mainEntity.name: Do I pay both state and local rates?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — the combined rate is state + county + city + special district. A "4 percent state tax" state can charge 9.5 percent combined in a high-rate city.

mainEntity.name: What changes when I cross state lines to buy?

acceptedAnswer.text: The seller charges the rate where the item is delivered, not where you live. Purchases in no-tax states still owe your state's use tax on bring-home items.

mainEntity.name: What is the simple interest formula?

acceptedAnswer.text: Interest = Principal × Rate × Time. For 10,000 dollars at 8 percent for 3 years: 10,000 × 0.08 × 3 = 2,400 dollars. Total repayment is principal plus interest.

mainEntity.name: How does simple interest differ from compound interest?

acceptedAnswer.text: Simple interest calculates only on the original principal. Compound interest adds earned interest to the base, so the interest accrues on interest. Over long terms the difference is substantial.

mainEntity.name: Where do you see simple interest in the US?

acceptedAnswer.text: Auto loans (accruing daily on the unpaid balance), short-term personal loans, some private promissory notes, and many bond coupons.

mainEntity.name: Is simple interest better for borrowers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, for the same APR and term — no "interest on interest" effect. Prepaying a simple-interest loan immediately stops further interest on the prepaid principal.

mainEntity.name: What is 365/360 interest accrual?

acceptedAnswer.text: A common commercial-loan convention where daily interest is calculated with a 360-day year denominator though 365 actual days pass. This slightly raises the effective rate — read the loan note carefully.

mainEntity.name: How much interest on 20,000 dollars at 6 percent for 5 years?

acceptedAnswer.text: 20,000 × 0.06 × 5 = 6,000 dollars. Total repayment 26,000 dollars — a monthly equal-amortization payment of 433.33 dollars over 60 months.

mainEntity.name: Can I prepay a simple-interest loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes—usually with no penalty on personal loans. The interest stops accruing on the prepaid portion the moment it is paid, unlike some precomputed-interest auto loans.

mainEntity.name: What is the Rule of 78s?

acceptedAnswer.text: An older precomputed-loan convention that front-loads interest heavily, penalizing early payoff. Banned on many consumer loans since 1993 but still seen in some subprime lending.

mainEntity.name: What is an AFR (Applicable Federal Rate)?

acceptedAnswer.text: The IRS minimum interest rate for below-market loans, set monthly. Family loans above the annual gift exclusion must charge at least AFR to avoid gift-tax implications.

mainEntity.name: Does simple interest mean no fees?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — origination fees, late fees, and prepayment penalties are separate charges. The APR (Annual Percentage Rate) reflects total cost including most fees.

us/student-loan-calculator.html.keywords: student loan calculator, student loan payment calculator, federal student loan payoff, student loan interest, standard repayment plan

mainEntity.name: Does this include income-driven repayment (IDR)?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. This calculator amortizes like a standard or extended repayment plan. IDR plans recompute payments each year based on income and family size, so amortization math doesn't apply.

mainEntity.name: Are loan forgiveness programs included?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF), Teacher Loan Forgiveness, and income-based forgiveness are separate programs; this calculator assumes the full balance is repaid.

mainEntity.name: How accurate is this calculator for private student loans?

acceptedAnswer.text: For fixed-rate private loans the math is the same. Variable-rate private loans change the payment every rate adjustment, so treat the result as a snapshot at today's rate.

mainEntity.name: What is the current federal student loan interest rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Undergraduate Direct loan rates reset every July 1 based on the 10-year Treasury auction — verify the current-year figure at studentaid.gov rather than assuming a fixed number.

mainEntity.name: Do I save money by paying extra each month?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Extra payments go straight to principal, reducing the interest that accrues afterwards. On a $35,000 loan at 5.5 percent, an extra $100 per month saves roughly $2,880 in interest and shortens payoff by about 2.5 years.

mainEntity.name: Should I refinance my student loans?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if you have stable income and don't need federal protections (IDR, PSLF, deferment). Refinancing federal loans into a private loan permanently gives up those protections.

mainEntity.name: What happens during a deferment or forbearance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Payments pause, but unsubsidized and private loans keep accruing interest. Subsidized federal loans may not accrue interest during deferment depending on the loan type and economic hardship status.

mainEntity.name: Can I deduct student-loan interest on my taxes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — the Student Loan Interest Deduction allows up to $2,500 per taxpayer per year, with income limits (MAGI phase-out; check current IRS rules). You don't need to itemize to claim it.

mainEntity.name: What is loan capitalization?

acceptedAnswer.text: Unpaid accrued interest gets added to the principal balance (capitalized) at certain events — end of grace period, end of deferment, IDR recertification events. It increases the balance you pay interest on going forward.

mainEntity.name: Does the standard repayment term have to be 10 years?

acceptedAnswer.text: Federal Direct loans default to 10-year standard repayment. Extended plans of 15, 20, or 25 years are available for balances above roughly $30,000, but longer terms pay more total interest.

mainEntity.name: How do I add or subtract hours and minutes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add directly (45 minutes + 30 minutes = 75 minutes = 1 hour 15 minutes). The calculator auto-normalizes the result.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between clock time and duration?

acceptedAnswer.text: Clock time is a point (3 PM); duration is a span (2 hours 15 minutes). Duration arithmetic doesn't carry AM/PM or day boundaries.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate time across midnight?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add 24 hours to the end time before subtracting. 10 PM to 2 AM is (2+24) − 22 = 4 hours.

mainEntity.name: What is 90 minutes in decimal?

acceptedAnswer.text: 1.5 hours. Payroll systems commonly use 1.5 rather than 1:30 for overtime calculations.

mainEntity.name: How many seconds in an hour?

acceptedAnswer.text: 3,600. In a day: 86,400. Useful when converting runtimes or batch durations to totals.

mainEntity.name: How do I sum multiple durations?

acceptedAnswer.text: Convert each to the same unit (minutes or seconds), sum, then re-convert. Standard practice in video editing and payroll.

mainEntity.name: Does Daylight Saving Time affect duration?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pure duration arithmetic ignores DST — a 3-hour span is still 3 hours. Clock-time transitions across a DST boundary add or lose an hour.

mainEntity.name: What is H:MM:SS?

acceptedAnswer.text: Standard notation for hours, minutes, seconds. 1:30:45 means one hour, thirty minutes, forty-five seconds.

mainEntity.name: How do I subtract a date and time together?

acceptedAnswer.text: Convert to a single unit (seconds since epoch or day-fraction) and subtract. This calculator supports date+time inputs.

mainEntity.name: How does video runtime work?

acceptedAnswer.text: Video durations use frame counts at 24/25/30/60 fps — often 23.976 fps in consumer submissions. Convert frames to seconds before summing with clock-time durations.

mainEntity.name: How many time zones does the continental US have?

acceptedAnswer.text: Four main: Eastern (ET), Central (CT), Mountain (MT), Pacific (PT). Including Alaska and Hawaii, plus territories, the US spans many more.

mainEntity.name: When does DST start and end in the US?

acceptedAnswer.text: Second Sunday in March at 2 AM (spring forward) and first Sunday in November at 2 AM (fall back). Arizona, Hawaii, and territories do not observe it.

mainEntity.name: What are the UTC offsets for each US zone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Standard: Eastern UTC-5, Central UTC-6, Mountain UTC-7, Pacific UTC-8. During DST: Eastern UTC-4, Central UTC-5, Mountain UTC-6, Pacific UTC-7.

mainEntity.name: Why doesn't Arizona observe DST?

acceptedAnswer.text: Extreme summer heat makes later sunset undesirable. Arizona stays on MST (UTC-7) year-round, except the Navajo Nation which does observe DST.

mainEntity.name: How do I schedule a meeting across US zones?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pick one reference ("2 PM ET") and translate. A 1 PM ET call is 10 AM PT and noon CT during standard time. Use calendar apps with explicit time zones.

mainEntity.name: Is 9 AM ET the same as 9 AM EST?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always — ET is the umbrella term; EST is winter-standard and EDT is summer-daylight. The calculator handles both.

mainEntity.name: How does crossing the International Date Line work?

acceptedAnswer.text: The date shifts (forward or backward) rather than just the time — Tokyo is UTC+9, so 9 AM Monday ET is 11 PM Monday in Tokyo.

mainEntity.name: What does "military time" mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 24-hour clock — 1300 is 1 PM, 0900 is 9 AM. Unambiguous for cross-zone scheduling.

mainEntity.name: What time is "noon" in each US zone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Noon local = 12 PM ET = 11 AM CT = 10 AM MT = 9 AM PT during standard time; shift an hour later during DST.

mainEntity.name: How do countries with half-hour offsets work?

acceptedAnswer.text: India (UTC+5:30), Nepal (+5:45), Iran (+3:30), and Afghanistan (+4:30) use fractional offsets. Add these when scheduling globally.

mainEntity.name: How do I solve a right triangle?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use the Pythagorean theorem a² + b² = c² plus sin/cos/tan for angles. Given any two of the three values, the rest follow.

mainEntity.name: What is SOH-CAH-TOA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sine = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent ÷ Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite ÷ Adjacent. The mnemonic for basic right-triangle trig.

mainEntity.name: What are degrees and radians?

acceptedAnswer.text: Degrees divide a circle into 360 parts; radians use π. 180° equals π radians. Stay consistent within one calculation.

mainEntity.name: What is the Law of Sines?

acceptedAnswer.text: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C — useful for ASA/AAS (two angles + a side) or SSA (flagging the ambiguous case).

mainEntity.name: What is the Law of Cosines?

acceptedAnswer.text: c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos C — a generalization of the Pythagorean theorem to non-right triangles. Used for SAS and SSS inputs.

mainEntity.name: What is Heron's formula?

acceptedAnswer.text: Area = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)) where s = (a+b+c)/2. Computes area from three side lengths without needing angles.

mainEntity.name: What is the area of a right triangle?

acceptedAnswer.text: ½ × base × height, where base and height are the two legs (not the hypotenuse).

mainEntity.name: What is the SSA ambiguous case?

acceptedAnswer.text: Given two sides and a non-included angle, there can be zero, one, or two valid triangles. The calculator flags this outcome.

mainEntity.name: How do I find a missing angle?

acceptedAnswer.text: Interior angles always sum to exactly 180°. Subtract the two known angles from 180.

mainEntity.name: What is the circumcircle?

acceptedAnswer.text: The unique circle through all three vertices; radius = a/(2·sin A). Its center is equidistant from all three corners.

mainEntity.name: What is a good APR for an auto loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: A good auto loan APR in the US typically ranges from 5% to 7% for new cars and 6% to 9% for used cars for borrowers with credit scores above 720.

mainEntity.name: How much down payment should I put on a car?

acceptedAnswer.text: The general recommendation is at least 20% down on a new vehicle and 10% on a used car to prevent negative equity as the vehicle depreciates.

mainEntity.name: How does vehicle trade-in affect sales tax?

acceptedAnswer.text: In most US states, trade-in credit reduces the taxable purchase price of the new vehicle. For example, trading an $8,000 car toward a $30,000 vehicle lowers taxable price to $22,000.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a 48, 60, and 72-month auto loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Shorter terms (36–48 months) have higher monthly payments but lower interest rates and drastically lower total interest costs. Longer terms (72–84 months) reduce monthly payments but increase total interest paid and risk negative equity.

mainEntity.name: Should I finance through a dealership, bank, or credit union?

acceptedAnswer.text: Credit unions and local banks frequently offer APRs 1% to 2% lower than dealership financing. Getting pre-approved before visiting the dealer gives you negotiating leverage and guards against dealer interest markups.

mainEntity.name: What is the 20/4/10 rule for buying a car?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 20/4/10 rule recommends putting at least 20% down, financing for no more than 4 years (48 months), and keeping total monthly transportation costs (loan, insurance, fuel) under 10% of gross monthly income.

mainEntity.name: What are typical dealer documentation and title fees?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dealer documentation fees ('doc fees') vary by state from $75 in New York and California to over $600 in Florida. Always ask for an itemized out-the-door price breakdown before signing.

mainEntity.name: Can I pay off my auto loan early without penalty?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most modern auto loans use simple interest and do not have prepayment penalties. Paying extra principal each month reduces future interest charges and shortens your payoff date.

mainEntity.name: Does a higher credit score lower car loan interest rates?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Super-prime borrowers (credit score 781+) qualify for the lowest rates (often 5%–6%), while subprime borrowers (score 501–600) can face rates of 12% to 18% or higher.

mainEntity.name: What is GAP insurance and do I need it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Guaranteed Asset Protection (GAP) insurance covers the gap between your car's market value and your remaining loan balance if the car is totaled or stolen. It is recommended if your down payment was under 20% or your loan term exceeds 60 months.
